# Visual reasoning task — woman in red and barrier arm

## Short answer

Yes. Assuming the woman in red stayed planted where she is standing in the video, she could have touched the red-and-white barrier arm next to her by raising her arm toward it.

## Who and what is being judged

- The woman in red is the woman in the red jacket and dark trousers who stands by the chain-link fence, immediately to the left of the man in the dark-blue suit and to the right of the left-hand white barrier housing. She is clearest in the first seconds, for example around 14:36:53–14:36:56, standing facing the fence with her back partly to the body camera.
- The barrier arm is the left-hand red-and-white striped arm that rises vertically from the white pedestal housing at the vehicle entrance. It is vertical because the gate is open, so it is a tall thin pole from about 1 m above the ground upward for several metres.
- “Without moving” is taken to mean feet stay planted and she does not walk, step sideways, jump, or lean her whole torso away from her spot. “By raising her arm” is taken to mean lifting one arm from rest to about shoulder height or higher, including reaching sideways-up toward the arm beside her, which is the natural way to touch something standing next to you.

## Why she could reach it

1. Height is not the obstacle. Because the arm is vertical, it is present at every height she can put her hand, from just above its white housing at about waist height up through head height and above. She does not need to reach something high overhead. She only needs to bridge the sideways horizontal gap at about shoulder-to-head height.

2. She stands on essentially the same ground plane and at essentially the same depth as the pedestal. Both stand on the same concrete entrance pad in front of the same chain-link fence. The top of the white housing comes to about her upper-leg to hip level, which is what is expected for a roughly 1 m housing next to a roughly 1.6 m adult at the same distance. If one were several metres behind the other, their apparent height ratio and their ground-contact positions would be visibly different, and they are not.

3. Camera motion confirms there is no hidden depth gap. As the body-worn camera shifts and turns through the first seconds, the pedestal-plus-arm and the woman shift together against the distant background of fence posts, utility pole, and power lines. The strip of fence and ground visible between the right side of the white housing and the left side of her red jacket stays narrow and stays present in view after view. That is what is expected for two objects side by side at the same depth. A large in-depth separation would have shown up as changing relative alignment, with the nearer object sliding past the farther one, and that does not happen.

4. That sideways gap is less than an arm length. In the image the edge-to-edge gap between housing and her torso is roughly two-thirds to one housing width, and the centre-to-centre distance from her torso to the arm is roughly one-and-a-half housing widths. A standard barrier housing is about 0.3–0.35 m wide, so the gap is on the order of 0.2–0.3 m edge to edge and about 0.5–0.65 m from her shoulder joint to the centreline of the arm. A normal adult woman’s shoulder-to-fingertip length is about 0.65–0.75 m, with maximum sideways reach from the body midline about 0.8 m. Her fingertips therefore extend past the line of the arm.

5. Raising the arm is enough. From rest, lifting the left arm sideways and slightly up to about shoulder or head height puts the hand at 1.4–1.8 m above the ground, where the vertical arm is still present just to her left. The lower part of the arm just above the housing is actually closest to her because perspective and lens geometry lean the top of the tall arm slightly away in the image, so she would touch the lower-to-mid portion, not the very top. No step, jump, or torso displacement is needed.

A strictly vertical overhead lift with the hand kept directly above the shoulder would still pass a few tens of centimetres to the side of the arm and would miss. That is not the natural reading of the question. Any normal attempt to touch the pole beside her would angle the raised arm sideways toward it, and that sideways-up raise bridges the gap.

Therefore, from her fixed standing position, raising her arm sideways-up toward the pole beside her would bring her hand to the line of the vertical red-and-white arm, and she could touch it.
